title: O my body
hook: the Guru speaks to the body: what have you done since you came into the world (Anand, the body pauris)

segments.voice: Yesterday, suniai, and your line, hear the true. Did one honest sentence come through the noise? Today the Anand stops talking about us and starts talking to us, part by part. Day three hundred ninety-four.

Halfway up a long flight of stairs, a man stops, puts a hand on his knee, and says out loud: come on, you can do this. People talk to their bodies all the time. We scold a stiff back, plead with a stomach before a big meeting, thank our legs at the end of a race. Usually it's a joke, or a complaint. Near the end of the Anand, Guru Amar Das does it too, on purpose, and the question he asks is not a joke. Today: sareeraa.
screen: `A MAN ON THE STAIRS: COME ON, KNEE.` → `WE ALL TALK TO OUR BODIES.` → `THE ANAND DOES IT ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Toward the close of the Anand comes a run of pauris that speak directly to parts of a person. The first begins ae sareeraa mairiaa: O my body. And then a question, in paraphrase: since you came into this world, what have you done? What deeds have you done, body, since you arrived? It sounds like an accusation, and it partly is. The pauri goes on: the One who fashioned you, you never kept in your mind. But it doesn't stop there. By the Guru's grace, it says, the Lord comes to dwell in the mind, and Guru Amar Das ends with a promise: the body that fixes its attention on the True Guru is accepted, approved, parvaan. So the question isn't a verdict. It's a mirror held up halfway through a life, with a way forward written underneath. Notice who is being asked. Not the soul, not the mind. The body. This pauri doesn't treat the body as a cage to escape. Elsewhere Guru Amar Das calls the body the Lord's temple, and Sikh life is lived in the body, as a householder: working, cooking, raising children, serving in langar with your own two hands. Uncut hair, kept as part of the Khalsa discipline, is explained by some as keeping the body as it was given. So the body isn't the problem in this pauri. It's the one being invited. Hands, feet, a whole lifetime of days: what will they be used for? O my body.
screen: `AE SAREERAA MAIRIAA: O MY BODY.` · `WHAT HAVE YOU DONE SINCE YOU CAME?` · `BY GRACE, THE BODY IS ACCEPTED.` · `NOT A CAGE: THE ONE BEING INVITED.` · then, large: `O MY BODY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank your body for one thing. Sit comfortably and let your attention move slowly from your feet up to your head. Somewhere along the way, stop at one part that did something for you today. The hands that made breakfast. The legs that carried you to the bus. The lungs, still going. Rest your attention there, and quietly say thank you to it, the way you'd thank a friend who helped you move house. Then breathe. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, and let it settle into that place. The bell holds the time.
Sareeraa, O body. Ae sareeraa mairiaa: the Anand asks the body what it has done in this world, and promises that the body turned toward the True Guru is accepted.
Your line: what have you done. Today, when you use your hands for something ordinary, washing a cup, carrying a bag, ask them quietly what they're doing it for. Day three hundred ninety-four.

screen: `DAY 394 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LIGHT PLACED IN YOU.`

howItsDone: These pauris are part of the full forty-pauri Anand Sahib, which many Sikhs recite each morning; the Sikh householder way lives faith out in the body, through work, family and service such as langar.

fork.setup: the pauri asks the body: what have you done since you came into the world? how does it end?
options: with grace: the body that turns to the True Guru is accepted.
by telling the body to leave the world behind.
fork.reveal: the question is a mirror, not a sentence: by the Guru's grace the Lord dwells in the mind, and that body is parvaan.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sareeraa, O body; the form Guru Amar Das uses when he speaks to the body in the Anand.

trapdoor: what you thought: O my body is a scolding: the body is the problem.
what it means: the body is asked what its days are for, and promised acceptance when it turns toward the True Guru.
what a scholar hears: the pauri is an apostrophe, a direct address, and it opens a sequence in the Anand that turns in the same way to the eyes and the ears.

sources.ref: Ramkali M3, Anand, the body pauri (ae sareeraa mairiaa, is jag meh aae kai), Ang 921–922
Prabhati M3 (harimandar eh sareer hai), Ang 1346

notes: The body pauri (ae sareeraa mairiaa is jag meh aae kai kiaa tudh karam kamaaiaa) paraphrased; commonly numbered pauri 34. Confirm numbering, Ang and the gloss of parvaan.
'Elsewhere Guru Amar Das calls the body the Lord's temple': harimandar eh sareer hai, attributed to Prabhati M3, Ang 1346. Confirm attribution and Ang.
Uncut hair 'often explained as keeping the body as it was given': a common Sikh explanation, not the only one. Confirm phrasing.
Review (2026-10-01): narrowed 'gurbani doesn't treat the body as a cage' to this pauri (gurbani also speaks of the body as fragile and passing); softened 'most of us' and 'often explained'.
